notes: Units can be miles, hours, tons, or any measurable output.
No time limit—depreciation stops when total units are reached or asset is retired.
formulaCard.title: Units-of-Production Formula
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Depreciation per Unit} = \frac{\text{Cost} - \text{Residual}}{\text{Total Estimated Units}}$$ $$\text{Annual Depreciation} = \text{Depreciation per Unit} \times \text{Units Used}$$

explanation: The [[kw:units‑of‑production method]] allocates depreciation based on how much the asset is used, not the passage of time.
Instead of years, the asset's life is expressed in total units of production (miles, hours, numbers of items produced).
Formula: $$\text{Depreciation per Unit} = \frac{\text{Cost} - \text{Residual Value}}{\text{Total Estimated Units}}$$.
Annual depreciation = Depreciation per unit × Units used during the year.
[[imp:This method is ideal for assets whose wear and tear is directly related to usage, like vehicles and machinery.]]

formulaCard.title: Schedule Computations
notes: Include all units up to the cap; do not exceed total depreciable cost.
If actual units exceed estimates, depreciation still stops at depreciable cost.
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Depreciation per Unit} = \frac{\text{Cost} - \text{Residual}}{\text{Total Estimated Units}}$$ $$\text{Annual Expense} = \text{Rate} \times \text{Units Used}$$ $$\text{Accumulated} = \sum \text{Expenses to Date}$$ $$\text{Book Value} = \text{Cost} - \text{Accumulated}$$

explanation: A [[kw:units‑of‑production depreciation schedule]] lists each year's usage, depreciation per unit, annual expense, accumulated depreciation, and book value.
The depreciation per unit is constant (just like straight‑line rate per unit).
The annual expense fluctuates with the actual units produced (or hours/miles).
The schedule continues until the total depreciable cost is fully allocated (or until the asset is retired).
[[imp:No depreciation is taken once the total estimated units are reached, even if the asset is still in use.]]

steps: Depreciation cannot exceed the depreciable cost.

examples.prompt: Explain why it's important to estimate total units accurately.
steps: If total units are under‑estimated, the depreciation rate will be too high; the asset will be fully depreciated too quickly.
If over‑estimated, the rate will be too low; the asset may still have a high book value even though it's worn out.
Either way, the expense won't match the actual economic use.

blocks.title: 3. Calculating Depreciation per Unit

visuals.caption: The rate is calculated once and used throughout the asset's useful life.
visuals.title: Examples of Depreciation per Unit

explanation: The [[kw:depreciation rate per unit]] is determined once, when the asset is acquired, based on estimated total units.
It is not changed unless there's a major revision to the estimate of total units or residual value.
Formula: $$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Cost} - \text{Residual}}{\text{Total Estimated Units}}$$.
This rate can be expressed in dollars per mile, per hour, per ton, per widget, etc.
[[imp:Accurate estimation of total units is critical because the rate affects every year's expense.]]

notes: Multiply actual units by rate each period.
formulaCard.title: Depreciation Rate per Unit

hints: The value at end of useful life.

blocks.title: 4. Comparing Units‑of‑Production to Straight‑Line

discoveryHook.scenario: If the same truck had been depreciated by straight‑line over 5 years, the expense each year would be ($30,000 – $5,000) ÷ 5 = $5,000. But actual miles varied, so units‑of‑production gives years of $5,000, $6,250, $3,750, etc., matching the uneven usage. Total depreciation is the same $25,000 under both methods.

visuals.caption: Same total depreciation, but different annual amounts.
visuals.title: Straight‑Line vs. Units‑of‑Production ($30,000 truck, residual $5,000)

explanation: Total depreciable cost is the same regardless of method; only the timing of expense recognition differs.
Straight‑line: equal expense each year, driven by time.
Units‑of‑production: variable expense, driven by usage.
Choosing the correct method depends on the nature of the asset and how it generates revenue.
[[imp:Both methods are GAAP‑compliant; the choice should reflect the pattern of economic benefits.]]

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Don't mix the two methods for the same asset. [[imp:Choose one method when the asset is acquired and stick with it consistently.]]

examples.title: B – When to use which
steps: A construction company's bulldozer may work 2,000 hours in a busy year and 500 in a slow year.
Units‑of‑production better matches the expense to the year's revenue because depreciation is tied to actual work done.
Straight‑line would under‑state expense in busy years and over‑state in slow years.
examples.prompt: Describe a situation where units‑of‑production would be more appropriate than straight‑line.

steps: No, total depreciation = depreciable cost = $20,000 under either method.
Only the timing of the expense differs.

explanation: Apply the blueprint to units‑of‑production depreciation:
1. Understand: identify asset cost, residual value, total estimated units, and actual units for the period.
2. Solve: compute the depreciation rate per unit; multiply by actual units to get annual expense; update accumulated depreciation and book value.
3. Conclude: verify that accumulated depreciation does not exceed depreciable cost; check that book value ≥ residual value.
This structure ensures you don't confuse the rate with the annual expense.

notes: Never let accumulated depreciation exceed depreciable cost.
If actual units exceed estimate, stop at depreciable cost.
